parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman calls a furniture company about a damaged delivery.
script: Good morning, HomeStyle Furniture customer service, Ryan speaking.
Hello. I'm calling about a delivery I received yesterday. There's a problem with it.
I'm sorry to hear that. Do you have your order number?
Yes, it's H T four five nine two.
Naomi Clarke. C, L, A, R, K, E.
I can see the order. It's a dining table, is that right?
Yes. The legs are fine, but the top is badly scratched. It must have happened during delivery.
I do apologise. Would you prefer a refund or a replacement?
A replacement, please. We really like the table, and we need it for a family dinner next week.
Of course. Can I confirm your address?
It's twenty-seven Beacon Road. B, E, A, C, O, N.
Thank you. We can deliver the new one on Thursday. Our drivers deliver either between eight and twelve, or between twelve and five.
The morning would be better, please.
So between eight and twelve on Thursday. The driver will also collect the damaged table, so please don't throw anything away.
And as an apology for the inconvenience, we'd like to offer you a voucher for thirty pounds to use on your next purchase.
You'll receive a confirmation of all this by email within the hour.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A volunteer coordinator talks to new volunteers at a community radio station.
script: Hi everyone, and welcome to Riverside FM. I'm Grace, the volunteer coordinator. Thank you so much for wanting to get involved.
A bit of background. The station started in 2010, broadcasting just a few hours a week from a room above a shop. Now we're on air twenty-four hours a day.
People often assume we're funded by advertising or by the council. In fact, most of our money comes from donations from our listeners. We have very little advertising.
All new volunteers begin with a training course over two weekends, where you'll learn how to use the equipment and the rules of broadcasting. Nobody presents a show until they've completed it.
We ask volunteers to commit at least four hours a week. That can be a single shift, or split across different days.
Let me tell you about some of our regular programmes, as you may want to help with one of them. Book Corner, where we interview local writers, is on Wednesdays.
Local Sport is on Sunday afternoons, with results from all the local clubs.
Youth Hour, presented by teenagers from local schools, goes out on Friday evenings.
Gardening Questions is on Sunday mornings. It's one of our most popular shows.
Jazz Night is late on Fridays, after Youth Hour.
And Health Talk, with doctors from the local hospital, is on Monday lunchtimes.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two architecture students, Mei and Ollie, discuss their design for student housing.
script: Mei, let's go over the brief for our student housing project again.
OK. The building has to house a hundred and twenty students, but the main requirement is energy efficiency. The judges want a building that uses as little energy as possible.
Right. And the site is going to be a challenge.
Yes, the biggest problem is that it slopes steeply towards the river. We'll have to design the building in steps.
What material should we use? I was thinking concrete.
Concrete has a huge carbon footprint. I'd prefer timber. Cross-laminated timber panels are strong enough for a building of five or six floors.
Timber it is. What about kitchens?
I don't think one big kitchen per floor works. Students prefer smaller shared kitchens, about one for every six students.
Good. And remember what Dr Clark said last time.
That we needed more natural light. Our first design was too dark.
Now, the extra features. I'd like a roof garden.
Definitely. It's good for insulation and for students' wellbeing. Let's include it.
There's a big university gym five minutes away, so let's leave that out.
Most students don't have cars, and it would be very expensive on this site. Leave it out.
But we must have bike storage.
I'm not sure. They take up a lot of space. Let's ask Dr Clark what she thinks.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of the spice trade.
script: Today we're going to look at the spice trade, and in particular at black pepper, which for centuries was one of the most valuable goods in the world.

Black pepper is native to south-west India, along what was known as the Malabar Coast. It was traded to the Mediterranean in ancient times, and the Romans used it in enormous quantities. When the Goths besieged Rome in the year 408, their demands reportedly included three thousand pounds of pepper.

It's often said that Europeans needed spices to hide the taste of rotten meat. Historians now reject this idea. Spices were far too expensive to waste on bad meat. Instead, they were used for flavour, and as a sign of wealth at the tables of the rich.

In the Middle Ages, spices reached Europe through a long chain of traders. Arab merchants brought them from India to ports in the Middle East, where they were bought by merchants from Venice, which grew rich by controlling much of the trade.
The desire to bypass these middlemen was a major motive for European voyages of exploration. In 1498, the Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama reached India by sailing around Africa.

Later, the Dutch East India Company fought brutally to control the trade in nutmeg, which grew only on the tiny Banda Islands in Indonesia. Nutmeg was so valuable that in 1667 the Dutch agreed to give the English the island of Manhattan in exchange for the small island of Run.
Chilli peppers, which are now used across Asia, came originally from the Americas, and only reached Asia in the sixteenth century.
Today, the largest producer of black pepper is not India but Vietnam. And scientists are studying piperine, the compound that gives pepper its heat, for possible anti-inflammatory effects.

passages.title: The First Flights
paragraphs: The first human flight did not take place in an aeroplane but beneath a balloon. Its inventors, Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier, were paper manufacturers from the town of Annonay in southern France. In 1782, Joseph noticed that a fire could make a light bag of fabric rise into the air, and the brothers began experimenting with larger and larger bags made of cloth lined with paper.

In June 1783, they gave their first public demonstration in Annonay, sending an unmanned balloon about 2,000 metres into the air. News of the experiment spread quickly, and in September they were invited to demonstrate their balloon at the royal palace of Versailles, in front of King Louis XVI. Because no one knew whether living creatures could survive at height, the first passengers were a sheep, a duck and a rooster. The balloon flew for about eight minutes and landed safely.

Encouraged by this success, the brothers prepared for a flight with human passengers. On 21 November 1783, Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes took off from Paris and flew for about 25 minutes, travelling around nine kilometres before landing safely outside the city. They had to keep feeding the fire with straw during the flight, and at one point had to put out small fires in the balloon's fabric.

Interestingly, the Montgolfiers did not fully understand why their balloons rose. They believed that the smoke from burning wet straw and wool produced a special gas with lifting power. In fact, it was simply the heated air, which is lighter than the cooler air around it. Only ten days after the first manned flight, the scientist Jacques Charles flew in a balloon filled with hydrogen, a gas much lighter than air, which could stay up for far longer.

Balloons soon found practical uses. During the French Revolutionary Wars, the French army formed a balloon corps, and in 1794, at the Battle of Fleurus, an officer in a tethered balloon was used for observation, reporting the movements of enemy troops.

Modern hot-air ballooning owes much to the American engineer Ed Yost, who in the 1950s developed balloons made of nylon and heated by burners using propane gas, making flights safer and easier to control. In 1999, Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones completed the first non-stop flight around the world by balloon, a journey of almost twenty days.

passages.title: The Trouble With Bees
paragraphs: Bees are among the most important animals on Earth for human food production. According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, around three-quarters of the world's leading food crops benefit to some degree from pollination by animals, most of all by bees. Without them, the supply of fruits, vegetables and nuts would fall sharply, and many foods would become far more expensive.

Public concern about bees grew rapidly in 2006, when beekeepers in the United States began reporting sudden and severe losses. Some lost between 30 and 90 percent of their hives over the winter. The pattern was unusual: the worker bees simply disappeared, leaving behind the queen, the young bees and stores of honey. The phenomenon was named colony collapse disorder.

No single cause has been identified, and most scientists now believe that several factors act together. One is the varroa mite, a parasite that feeds on bees and spreads viruses among them. Another is a group of pesticides called neonicotinoids, which can affect bees' ability to navigate and find food. After reviewing the evidence, the European Union banned the outdoor use of the three main neonicotinoids in 2018.

Much of the public discussion has focused on honeybees, which are managed by beekeepers and whose numbers can be restored relatively quickly. Yet honeybees are just one of around 20,000 species of bee worldwide. Many wild bees, including bumblebees and solitary bees, are important pollinators, and several species have declined severely. Because they are not managed and are harder to count, their decline has received much less attention.

One of the most serious threats to wild bees is the loss of their habitat. In the United Kingdom, for example, around 97 percent of wildflower meadows have been lost since the 1930s, largely as a result of changes in farming. Without a variety of flowers through the spring and summer, many bees cannot find enough food.

There are encouraging signs of action. Many farmers now plant wildflower strips along the edges of fields, and some councils allow roadside verges to grow wild rather than mowing them regularly. Urban beekeeping has also become popular, but scientists warn that it is not always helpful: where hives are too numerous, honeybees may compete with wild bees for limited flowers. For wild bees, planting flowers is often more useful than keeping more honeybees.

passages.title: Is Homework Worth It?
paragraphs: Few aspects of school life cause as much disagreement as homework. Some parents complain that their children are given too much, leaving little time for play, sport or family. Others worry that schools which set little homework are failing to prepare students properly. Teachers themselves are often divided.

The most comprehensive analysis of the research was carried out by the American psychologist Harris Cooper. In a review published in 2006, he and his colleagues found a clear link between homework and achievement for older students, but a much weaker one for children in primary school. Cooper has suggested a guideline sometimes called the '10-minute rule': about ten minutes of homework per night for each year of school, so twenty minutes for a child in the second year and two hours for a student in the final year of secondary school.

Supporters of less homework often point to Finland, whose students have performed well in international tests despite being given relatively little homework. However, it would be a mistake to conclude from this that homework is unnecessary. Finland's success has many causes, including highly trained teachers and a strong social welfare system, and countries such as South Korea and Singapore have also done well with very different approaches.

There is evidence that too much homework can be harmful. A 2013 study by Denise Pope and colleagues at Stanford University surveyed students at high-achieving schools in wealthy communities in California, where students reported more than three hours of homework a night on average. Many reported high levels of stress, as well as physical symptoms such as headaches and sleep problems.

Homework can also increase inequality. Students whose parents can help them, and who have a quiet place to work and reliable internet access, are at a clear advantage over those who share crowded homes or must look after younger siblings. Some schools have responded with 'flipped' classrooms, in which students watch short video lessons at home and do the practice tasks, traditionally given as homework, in class where teachers can help.

In my view, the evidence does not support abolishing homework altogether, particularly for older students preparing for exams. But it should be limited, purposeful and clearly connected to what is being learned in class. For younger children, I believe the most valuable activity at home is simply reading for pleasure, which has well-established benefits and rarely causes stress.

task1.text: The line graph below shows the average age of women when they had their first child in four countries between 1980 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

chart.title: Average age of mothers at first birth

model: The line graph shows the average age at which women in Japan, the UK, the USA and Brazil had their first child between 1980 and 2020.
Overall, the average age of first-time mothers rose steadily in all four countries. Japan had the highest figure throughout the period, while Brazil consistently had the lowest.
In 1980, Japanese women had their first child at an average age of 26, slightly older than British women at 25. Mothers in the USA and Brazil were younger, at 23 and 22 respectively.

Over the next four decades, the figures for Japan, the UK and the USA increased by around one year per decade, although Japan's rise accelerated after 2000, reaching 31 in 2020, five years higher than in 1980. The UK figure reached 29 and the USA's 27. Brazil remained at 22 until 1990 but then rose more quickly, especially between 2010 and 2020, ending the period at 26, the same age that Japanese mothers had been in 1980.

task2.text: Some people say that modern technology, such as smartphones and social media, is making people less sociable. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: It is common to see groups of friends sitting together in a café, each looking at their own phone. Scenes like this have led many people to argue that technology is making us less sociable. I partly agree: technology has reduced some kinds of face-to-face interaction, but it has also created new ways of connecting with others.

There is evidence that heavy use of smartphones can damage social life. When people constantly check their phones during conversations, the quality of those conversations tends to suffer, and others may feel ignored. Social media can also replace real relationships with superficial ones, in which people collect hundreds of online 'friends' but have few people they can talk to honestly. Some studies have linked heavy social media use among teenagers to loneliness and anxiety.

On the other hand, technology allows people to stay in touch in ways that were impossible a generation ago. Families separated by migration can see each other every day on video calls, and students who move to a new country can maintain friendships from home. Online communities also allow people with unusual interests or disabilities to find others like themselves. For shy people in particular, messaging can be an easier first step towards friendship.

In my view, technology itself is not the problem; the way it is used is what matters. When devices replace face-to-face contact, they make people less sociable, but when they support and extend real relationships, they can make us more connected.

In conclusion, although I agree that technology can reduce the quality of social interaction, I believe it is up to individuals to use it in ways that strengthen, rather than replace, their relationships.

speaking.cue:
Describe a photograph or painting that you like.
You should say:
- what it shows
- where you saw it
- why it was taken or made
and explain why you like it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to describe a photograph that hangs on the wall of my room at home. It shows my grandparents standing in front of their house in the village, on the day they got married, which was more than fifty years ago. It's black and white, a bit faded, and slightly damaged in one corner, because it survived a flood in the nineteen-eighties. In the photo, my grandmother is wearing a dark sari, and my grandfather looks very serious, almost nervous, which makes me laugh because he's always been such a cheerful person. Behind them, you can see a big mango tree that still stands in the same place today. The photo was taken by a travelling photographer who visited the village a few times a year, because hardly anyone owned a camera in those days. I like it for several reasons. Firstly, it's a direct link to my family's history, and every time I look at it, I think about how different their lives were from mine. Secondly, I find old photos more meaningful than the thousands of pictures we take on our phones today. Because it was the only photo they had of that day, it feels precious, and I think that's something we've lost.
